transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2028-03-12
- Start: 14:30 UTC
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Summary:
Silverstrand is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + private options. Primary drivers: very long document context (60k-100k tokens for downhole logs and regulatory docs), robust multilingual support (Finnish + Hindi + Spanish, plus code-switching in field notes), and tool-calling to their billing API and an internal doc retrieval service. They want to understand tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) for cost, latency, and compliance. SE asked about quantization profiles and prefix KV caching. Customers requested a pilot to run NER/QA and a throughput/latency check.

Topics discussed:
- Context length requirements and token budgeting
- Multilingual model behavior & code-switching
- Tool-calling patterns and auth for private endpoints
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
- Benchmark plan and next steps

Questions noted:
- How does Redwood handle 100k token KV caches?
- Can we call customer-hosted tools inside Redwood Private (VPC) securely?
- Cost delta between hosted per-token vs reserved dedicated pools?

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick roll call?
[00:06] Anika (Silverstrand): hi, Anika here, head of AI. we've got Rajiv and Lena on the line as well.
[00:11] Rajiv: morning all.
[00:12] Diego (Redwood SE): Diego here, I'll focus on the technical bits — happy to dig into latency and caching.
[00:17] Maya: perfect. goal today — understand your context length needs, multilingual constraints, and tool-calling so we can propose hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:27] Anika: great. high level — we run post-drilling reports, long regulatory docs, and operator field logs. typical user session might include a 30k-80k token compound doc, sometimes up to ~100k for combined corpora.
[00:42] Lena: and we have heavy finnish and hindi content in some regions, plus field notes where engineers switch between english and their local language mid-sentence — code-switching.
[00:54] Tomás (SRE): security is key; some logs are PII-adjacent. we need audit logs, SSO, and ideally customer-managed keys.
[01:03] Diego: okay, that's helpful. our runtime supports long-context via prefix caching and KV management; but practicality depends on the model's architecture and memory when you push to 100k tokens. question — are you doing streaming token-by-token QA or batch jobs?
[01:18] Rajiv: mostly interactive sessions, engineers want snappy responses for QA and summarization queries during shifts. peak concurrency is ~25-40 users during windows, with bursts to 100 QPS for short intervals.
[01:32] Diego: good to know. for low-latency interactive use with large context we often recommend model sharding strategies + aggressive prefix caching. for hosted, we can keep a warm pool and use KV cache for repeated prefixes. for dedicated you get reserved pools which make KV cache hits more predictable.
[01:51] Anika: what about private? we prefer private for regulatory zones, but hosting on-prem increases ops burden.
[01:58] Maya: correct, private gives you the control — VPC with our private control plane or on-prem bundle. Diego, maybe explain auth for tool-calling in private?
[02:07] Diego: sure — in Private deployments you can configure internal tool endpoints reachable only within your VPC; Redwood's callout layer supports mTLS + per-route credentials. for hosted we proxy tool calls with secure tokens, but some customers prefer direct VPC peering to their doc-store.
[02:23] Rajiv: we need tool-calling to two systems: our billing API (sensitive) and an internal doc retrieval service behind a VPC. how do you manage secrets?
[02:32] Diego: we integrate with KMS/HSM — keys are customer-managed in Private. hosted also supports KMS but we manage the key wrapping; for strict compliance you can request HSM-backed keys in Private.
[02:44] Tomás: okay. on the model side, we're evaluating open models. we've benchmarked a few locally (LargeBase, MistralX variants). what's Redwood's guidance on quantization and multilingual behavior?
[02:58] Diego: open models vary — some quantize gracefully to int8 or 4-bit with tiny accuracy loss; others degrade on non-Latin languages. we maintain a model catalog and performance profiles — for long-context multilingual tasks, models with native multi-token and good Unicode handling tend to fare better. we can suggest a shortlist after seeing your sample data.
[03:18] Anika: ideal — can you do a small eval on our Finnish and Hindi snippets? we want to see how NER and QA perform, plus hallucination rate.
[03:27] Maya: absolutely. Diego will set up a pilot harness. Diego, rough ETA?
[03:31] Diego: I can have the initial benchmark config and a small harness by Friday, assuming we get the samples tomorrow.
[03:36] Rajiv: we'll push samples by end of day tomorrow.
[03:39] (small cross talk)
[03:42] Lena: one nuance — Finnish uses a lot of compound words; models sometimes split tokens oddly which screws NER. we need to measure entity extraction F1, not just BLEU.
[03:52] Diego: noted — we'll measure NER F1 and QA exact-match. also we'll include some code-switched examples to check tokenization consistency.
[04:02] Anika: what about context windows — does Redwood stitch long documents or do you rely on model context only?
[04:09] Diego: our runtime supports stitching via summarization + prefix caching. two approaches: 1) windowing with overlapping segments and an aggregator, or 2) using a long-context model (if available) plus KV cache. For 100k tokens, typically we use hierarchical retrieval + augmentation to avoid hitting single-model memory limits.
[04:31] Rajiv: latency tradeoffs? engineers expect under 1s for short queries, but we're realistic — with 50k tokens maybe 2-3s is acceptable.
[04:40] Diego: depends on model size and quantization. With a trimmed model + dedicated pool we can get interactive latencies in that ballpark for moderate-size models. For very long context we often accept slightly higher latencies unless we do caching or pre-aggregation.
[04:56] Maya: to summarize: we'll propose two pilot lanes — hosted warm pool (fast onboard, higher per-token cost), and dedicated reserved pool for predictable latency/cost. Private will be scoped if compliance requires on-prem or VPC peering.
[05:09] Tomás: also send SOC2 docs and the audit log retention options — legal will want that before any pilot.
[05:16] Maya: yes — we'll attach those.
[05:18] Anika: one more on tool-calling: can Redwood support multi-step tool flows where the model calls the doc service and then calls billing? transactionality is important.
[05:30] Diego: we can orchestrate multi-step flows — function calling + tool orchestration. for transactional sequences we recommend an orchestration layer on your side for final commits, Redwood handles the model-determined steps and returns structured outputs. in Private you can tighten auth between steps.
[05:46] Rajiv: pricing — what's a rough delta? hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved?
[05:50] Maya: rough rule of thumb: hosted is higher per-token but zero infra ops; dedicated is lower unit cost with monthly commitment. we'll send a tailored pricing sheet with sample traffic and cost modeling.
[06:02] Lena: do you support multilingual fine-tuning or is it mostly prompts/PEFT?
[06:08] Diego: we support fine-tuning and PEFT workflows in Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports prompt engineering and few-shot; some hosted offerings allow customer-tuned models via our managed fine-tuning program — depends on contract.
[06:22] Anika: curious about how Redwood handles KV cache eviction for long-running sessions — we have shift-long sessions that might accumulate state.
[06:31] Diego: cache eviction is policy-driven — LRU by default, and we expose hooks to pin prefixes for premium tiers. for dedicated you can reserve more memory and tweak policies.
[06:44] Tomás: on-metrics — can we get token-level cost and latency traces per user?
[06:50] Maya: yes, the Console has token-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. Diego can show a sample dashboard during the pilot.
[07:00] Diego: I'll include a short walkthrough in the pilot onboarding doc.
[07:04] (brief silence)
[07:08] Anika: ok, timeline — we'd like a pilot next week if possible, with initial results the following week.
[07:15] Maya: we'll aim for that. Diego will prepare harness, we'll send pricing and security artifacts, and Rajiv will send samples.
[07:23] Rajiv: sounds good.
[07:25] Maya: any other concerns?
[07:27] Lena: just to double-check tokenization edge cases and how you'll measure hallucination across languages.
[07:34] Diego: included in scope — we'll run hallucination tests and entity overlap metrics.
[07:39] Tomás: one ops note — if we go Private we need an install window for the on-prem bundle; let's leave that for the pilot decision.
[07:48] Maya: yep.
[07:50] (wrap)
[07:52] Maya: recap of next steps: pricing + security docs by Friday, benchmark harness config by Friday, samples from Silverstrand by tomorrow, schedule SE benchmark call next week.
[07:58] Anika: thanks everyone. we'll be in touch.
[08:01] Diego: thanks all.
[08:03] (call ends)

Notes about transcription fidelity: occasional homophones ("K V cash" vs "KV cache"), proper nouns may be slightly off — e.g., model names noted in the call (LargeBase) may differ from canonical upstream names. Action items and next steps captured above.
